subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Pan-Roasting: The Ancient Method
description: Learn Pan-Roasting: The Ancient Method in one minute.

hook.text: For 500 years, coffee was roasted in a simple pan over open fire—stirred by hand, judged by eye and nose.

buildup.text: Ethiopian and Yemeni coffee traditions still use this method. A flat pan over charcoal, constant hand stirring.

discovery.text: Pan roasting is inconsistent—some beans burn while others stay raw. But it's deeply personal and richly aromatic.

twist.text: In Ethiopia's coffee ceremony, guests watch the entire pan-roasting process. The smoke is fanned toward them as a welcome.

climax.text: Pan roasting connects drinkers to the transformation moment. Industrial roasting hides what pan roasting celebrates.

punchline.text: A pan, a fire, a hand. Coffee's oldest roasting method is still alive.

quiz.question: Why is pan-roasting still practiced in Ethiopian coffee ceremonies?
options: It connects drinkers to the visible transformation—the smoke is part of the welcome

details.summary: Pan roasting is one of the oldest coffee preparation methods, still practiced in Ethiopia and parts of the Middle East. Green beans are placed in a flat metal pan over an open flame and stirred constantly by hand. The result is rustic, uneven, and deeply traditional.
details.whyItMatters: Pan roasting connects modern coffee drinkers to centuries of tradition. It demonstrates that great coffee does not require expensive machines, just attention and care.
takeaways: Pan roasting uses a flat pan over open flame with constant stirring
It is still practiced traditionally in Ethiopia and the Middle East
Results are characteristically uneven and richly aromatic

faq.question: How does the flavor of pan-roasted coffee compare to drum-roasted?
faq.answer: Pan-roasted coffee tends to be smokier and more uneven, with a range of roast levels in a single batch. This creates a complex, rustic flavor profile that is distinctly different from the uniform taste of drum-roasted beans.

faq.question: Can you pan-roast coffee at home with kitchen equipment?
faq.answer: Yes. A cast iron skillet or wok over medium-high heat works well. Stir constantly for ten to fifteen minutes until the beans reach your desired color, then cool them immediately in a colander with shaking.
